strengths: Addresses a fundamental and well-motivated problem: exposure bias in autoregressive robot world models, with clear motivation and compelling examples
Solid theoretical contribution with rigorous derivation of convergence guarantees for x0-prediction parameterization; Theorem 1 is formally proven
Novel variable-length prefix branching protocol elegantly solves the challenge of generating comparable candidates in autoregressive video generation

Comprehensive experimental validation with multiple complementary approaches: quantitative metrics across 3 camera views, task-relevant masked evaluations, blind human study with ELO ranking, policy evaluation on real tasks, and extensive ablations
Strong empirical results: 14% LPIPS reduction, 9.1% SSIM improvement, 98% paired comparison win rate, 80% human preference with statistical significance (p<10^-20)
Practical and well-designed multi-view visual rewards with group normalization addressing key challenges in sparse reward learning
Clear presentation with effective figures, detailed algorithm, complete derivations, and reproducible implementation details
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contrastive RL objective adapted from DiffusionNFT [42]; exposure bias is well-known problem from sequence generation literature; concurrent work [36] pursues similar approach
Evaluation scope restricted to single dataset (DROID) with single robot platform; lacks multi-dataset validation and comparison with other recent RL-based world model methods
Significant computational overhead during post-training (K=16 candidates per update, 3 days on 8 H200 GPUs) without detailed cost-benefit analysis or comparison with simpler alternatives
Empirical improvements, while consistent, are incremental (10-15% range on most metrics) rather than transformative
Requires access to held-out ground truth for reward computation, limiting applicability in some scenarios; visual metrics are proxies without explicit physical plausibility constraints

Limited technical justification: Theorem 1 assumes unlimited data/capacity; connection between theoretical improvement direction and practical visual quality metrics somewhat loose; why x0-prediction specifically benefits not thoroughly explained
Human study uses only 8 in-house expert raters with moderate inter-rater agreement (κ~0.4); generalization limited; no crowd-sourced validation

Narrow scope of applicability: only tabletop manipulation, limited rollout lengths (11s), unclear generalization to other embodiments/architectures; variable-length prefix strategy assumes specific model structure
Missing comparisons with simpler exposure bias solutions (scheduled sampling, curriculum learning); no ablation of β hyperparameter

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing exposure bias in autoregressive robot world models with clear practical importance
Rigorous theoretical contribution: sound adaptation of contrastive RL (DiffusionNFT) to x0-prediction with complete derivation and proven convergence guarantees

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation including quantitative metrics, paired comparisons (98% win rate), human preference study (80%, Elo 884.8 vs 715.2), task-centric ablations, generalization to multiple datasets, policy evaluation correlation, and policy improvement experiments

Thoughtful algorithmic design: variable-length prefix sampling cleverly exposes diverse error regimes; group-relative training well-adapted to autoregressive video; multi-view rewards improve task-relevant performance
Substantial practical improvements: 14% LPIPS reduction on external cameras, 9.1% SSIM improvement on wrist camera; qualitative results show objects maintaining integrity over 11-second rollouts
Extensive ablation studies (Tables 3-11) thoroughly justify design choices including learning rate, reward signals, prefix strategy, group size, and prediction horizon
Excellent presentation with clear figures, comprehensive appendix (38 pages with derivations, ablations, human study details, and algorithm pseudocode)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution is adapting existing method (DiffusionNFT [47]) from velocity-prediction to x0-prediction; while technically sound, this is somewhat incremental

Computational cost inadequately characterized: paper states '2 days on 8 H200 GPUs' but provides no timing comparison to baseline fine-tuning; K=16 candidates implies ~16x inference overhead during post-training; cost-benefit analysis missing
Limited model/dataset exploration in depth: Ctrl-World is primary focus; Bridge and RT-1 experiments are brief (100k step fine-tune then post-train only)
Reward design lacks novelty: straightforward weighted combination of LPIPS, SSIM, PSNR; Table 13 shows superiority over HPSv3 but this reflects appropriateness rather than novel engineering

Modest downstream task improvements relative to visual gains: 19% policy improvement on single 4-block picking task is the only downstream evaluation; unclear if visual quality consistently translates to policy learning benefits

Limited comparisons to concurrent related work: WorldCompass [41] uses similar contrastive RL paradigm but lacks direct comparison; Self-Forcing comparison uses custom baseline rather than published implementation
Theoretical results are intuitive: Theorem 1 essentially states model learns reward-aligned direction; while x0-adaptation is correct, core insight is not novel
Design choices lack principled justification: K=16, F=1, β choices not systematically ablated; some hyperparameters (reward weights in Table 6) appear somewhat arbitrary
No failure mode analysis: paper doesn't explore when method struggles or provide negative results; limited discussion of when RL post-training might degrade performance
Human study could be more rigorous: 8 expert raters with κ≈0.4 inter-rater agreement; while statistically significant, larger participant pool and lay-person evaluation would strengthen claims
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; hyperparameter choices lack principled justification; custom human evaluation platform reduces replicability

Limited analysis of generalization: unclear how performance degrades beyond 70-frame rollouts; transfer to different action distributions and task domains not explored; sim-to-real deployment not demonstrated
